infrastructureContract.composition: Private nested DelayState owns a new Task, optional TimerHandle and CancellationTokenRegistration, plus a resource lock and cleanupRequested marker. Task remains final. Place helper implementations nested/private, or a package-private TaskDelaySupport.java only if size requires it. No public nested interfaces, setters, constructors or cancellation producer escapes.
interfaces: Private DelayTimer.schedule(long milliseconds, Runnable callback) -> idempotent TimerHandle.cancel()

Per-invocation registration function mapping token/callback to the actual CancellationTokenRegistration, production using token.Register(Action); the test function gates before/after the real registration and returns that real CTR, never subclasses the final carrier
Per-invocation asynchronous Executor for delay completion/continuations
Package-private test entry point accepting an immutable per-call infrastructure object, never a global mutable hook
infrastructureContract.productionTimer: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor with remove-on-cancel enabled and one scheduler worker is acceptable only for expiry notification. Scheduled work hands off to independent cached daemon workers and returns immediately; no arbitrary user continuation executes on the scheduler worker. Use java.base only. Native source supports callback threadpool dispatch; there is no exact thread-count or latency equivalence claim.
infrastructureContract.rejection: Define a delay-specific rejected-executor fallback using a fresh noninheriting daemon worker, so neither cancellation nor timer scheduler executes user continuations inline on rejection. Preserve exactly-once completion/dispatch attempts. Catastrophic allocation failure is not a fabricated native fault mapping; retain raw failure and make cleanup best-effort in finally.
infrastructureContract.construction: Create DelayState before invoking scheduling; finite timer may call back before schedule returns. Publish returned handle under resource lock, then dispose it outside lock if cleanupRequested or Task already terminal. Register cancellation only for cancelable non-fastpath promises; callback may run synchronously before Register returns. Publish returned CTR with the same late-publication rule. If setup throws after acquiring a resource, detach and dispose acquired resources before rethrowing the setup failure; do not fabricate a faulted Task for runtime infrastructure failure.
infrastructureContract.cleanup: Winning timer calls completion first, then cleanup; winning cancellation completes then cleanup. Use finally around completion dispatch so unexpected dispatch failure cannot skip cleanup once terminal. Cleanup atomically marks cleanupRequested and detaches published handles under resource lock; outside all Delay/Task locks dispose registration then timer. Each late-published resource observes terminal/cleanupRequested and disposes itself outside the lock. Idempotent handle/CTR disposal permits duplicate paths safely. Record the winning attempt before continuation dispatch inside the Task terminal transition (a private per-attempt outcome holder, never a public callback). Only that winner owns completion-finally cleanup; terminal status alone is not proof this caller won. Late-publication disposal remains a separate constructor obligation. This distinguishes a loser from a winner whose dispatch subsequently throws.
infrastructureContract.lockOrder: Never wait in CTR.Dispose while holding Delay resource lock or Task lock. Never hold resource lock across scheduling, registration, completion or arbitrary callback invocation. Source Cancel already releases CTS lock before callbacks. Cancellation cleanup can dispose its own registration without waiting; external timer cleanup can wait for an in-flight cancellation callback only while owning no locks the callback needs.
infrastructureContract.completionBeforeCleanup: Terminal status can precede cleanup while an inline timer continuation blocks. Require eventual resource cleanup after that continuation is released, not eager cleanup at the first status observation. Late constructor publication may independently dispose its returned resource while the winning continuation is still running; both orders are source-permitted.
infrastructureContract.retention: Canceled scheduled futures are removed from the queue. Detach resource fields after cleanup. Keep the public Task from retaining a completed DelayState unnecessarily; callback closures may retain it only until timer work/registration is released. No forced-GC timing acceptance assertion.

phaseDiscipline.seams: Immutable infrastructure supplied only to a per-call package-private entry. Fake scheduler can invoke callback before returning handle, pause at publication, expose idempotent dispose count and release its own gate. Fake registrar can cancel token then synchronously invoke callback before returning the actual CTR. Use actual CTR for self-dispose/external-wait controls. A queued executor can hold and release individual continuations without modifying global Task behavior.
phaseDiscipline.phaseControl: CountDownLatch/CyclicBarrier/Semaphore or native ManualResetEventSlim gates with timeouts; signal entered, release, returned and cleanup-complete phases. Every acquired gate is released in finally and every owned worker joined or terminated within the process budget. Do not block the same thread that must produce the release signal. An entered-intent signal alone is not proof that Dispose blocked. Require explicit return/release ordering with a controlled callback still active, and classify any negative-at-sample observation honestly.
phaseDiscipline.nativeLimits: Native public APIs cannot force internal timer-field races. Capture only stable public observations; deterministic publication/cleanup race proofs are Java-only source-derived controls, not invented native observations.
phaseDiscipline.envelopes: Per-phase waits at most 2 seconds; use separate bounded groups/processes where needed so aggregate native execution remains within 30 seconds and Java within 120 seconds. Finite timer smoke uses a short nominal delay plus a generous 2-second completion envelope, without asserting exact elapsed milliseconds or ordering across unrelated timers. Infinite pending proof relies on branch/resource control and bounded handshakes, not a long sleep.
phaseDiscipline.wire: Versioned stable keys and strict typed Boolean/int/string observations. Add int64 encoding only if the schema explicitly defines it, otherwise serialize tick inputs as canonical strings. No absolute timestamps, exact thread IDs, addresses, scheduler latency or random ordering in equality comparisons. Race rows express allowed outcome invariants instead of requiring one native winner to repeat in Java.
